deep.reconstruction:
Setting. Σ̲ = (X, Σ) is a cellular surface: a pseudo-line arrangement on a surface X, presumably the projective plane, with vertex set S(Σ). Grothendieck considers the space of 'relative positions' of an additional pseudo-line D with respect to Σ. He writes it X* = Bal(Σ̲); 'Bal' plausibly abbreviates 'balayage', i.e. sweeping. He treats X* as a cellular surface, stratified much like the dual of a point configuration in the plane:
- Faces of X* are 'stable' positions Δ: D passes through no vertex of Σ.
- Edges are 'sous-stable' (sub-stable) positions L: D passes through exactly one vertex s.
- Vertices are 'critical' positions ρ: D_ρ passes through several vertices, the set S_ρ = D_ρ ∩ S(Σ).

Local structure at a vertex ρ.
- A local orientation of X* at ρ corresponds to an orientation of D_ρ.
- The outgoing edges at ρ correspond to pairs (s, ω), with s ∈ S_ρ and ω a rotation sense at s.
- To (s, ω) corresponds the sub-stable position D_{ρ,s,ω}. It is obtained by keeping D through s, turning it slightly in sense ω, and releasing all the other vertices of S_ρ. This gives the edge a_{s,ω}.
- So a vertex lying on k vertices of Σ has degree 2k, exactly as for a line through k points in the classical dual arrangement.
- He then considers the next edge b_{s,ω} in the cyclic order around ρ. Passing from a_{s,ω} to b_{s,ω} corresponds to switching from the 'left' generalisation of D_{s,ω} at s to the 'right' one. This describes the face-circuits around ρ.

The real difficulty. Grothendieck observes that the local study of X* near a vertex, or near a face Δ, is easy. The conceptual difficulty lies near an edge a_L, given by a sub-stable L through a single vertex s.
- The two incident faces F_Δ and F_Δ' are easy: they are the two generalisations of L at s.
- The hard part is to determine the two endpoint vertices of a_L intrinsically. These are the critical positions reached by 'rotating' L about s until it becomes blocked by further vertices of Σ.
- He notes how the orientations match up. An orientation of a_L amounts to an orientation of L together with a rotation sense ω_s at s. Equivalently it amounts to a choice of one of the two incident faces.
- The aim is to describe the endpoint of the oriented edge (a, ω_a) in terms of (L, ω_s): as the critical position deduced from the position 'bloquée' around s, given the orientation of the corresponding piece of L − {s}.
- He stops with: 'L'ennui, c'est qu'il y a plusieurs choix naturels qui viennent à l'esprit, et qu'il n'est pas sûr qu'aucun ...' — the rest is barely legible. For pseudo-lines there is no canonical rotation, so several natural candidate rules exist, and it is unclear whether any of them yields a well-defined cell structure making X* a surface.

Purpose. This builds a cellular, 2-dimensional 'dual' or extension complex of a pseudo-line arrangement: a combinatorial model for the space of pseudo-lines that can be added to Σ. In modern terms this is close to the extension space of a rank-3 oriented matroid, or to the configuration space underlying topological sweeps.
errors: Nothing outright false is asserted. The sticking point Grothendieck himself flags is real: the endpoints of an edge a_L (the 'next' critical positions on rotating a pseudo-line about s) are not canonically defined geometrically. A purely combinatorial definition is needed, e.g. via sign vectors or cocircuit signatures; with it, the face poset is well defined but it is no longer obvious that X* is a surface.
Calling X* a 'surface cellulaire' presupposes a manifold property. For the analogous oriented-matroid extension spaces this is a non-trivial matter, not something automatic.

ideas.what: Space X* = Bal(Σ) of relative positions of an added pseudo-line with respect to an arrangement Σ, with a cell structure: stable positions are faces, positions through one vertex are edges, positions through several vertices are vertices.
ideas.modern_name: Extension space / poset of one-element extensions of a rank-3 oriented matroid (pseudo-line arrangement); combinatorial dual arrangement
ideas.usually_credited_to: Las Vergnas (single-element extensions via cocircuit signatures, 1978); Sturmfels–Ziegler, 'Extension spaces of oriented matroids' (1993); Goodman–Pollack on extensions and sweeps
ideas.where_published: Pseudo-line arrangements are only alluded to in Esquisse d'un programme / Récoltes et Semailles; no published treatment of X*.

ideas.what: Local structure at a critical vertex: outgoing edges ↔ pairs (vertex s on D_ρ, rotation sense ω); local orientation of X* ↔ orientation of D_ρ; vertex degree 2|S_ρ|.
ideas.modern_name: Local structure of the dual (extension) complex at a point of multiplicity k
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical projective duality, extended combinatorially (Goodman–Pollack, oriented matroid theory)

ideas.what: Identification of the edge-endpoint problem — 'rotating' a pseudo-line about a vertex until it is blocked — as the conceptual core, with the observation that several natural non-equivalent rules exist.
ideas.modern_name: Elementary moves / pseudo-line rotation (allowable sequences, topological sweep)

missed.claim: Grothendieck sets up, around 1983–84 and independently of the oriented-matroid literature, a cellular surface parametrising the pseudo-lines extendable to a given arrangement, and he expects it to be a surface. This is essentially the rank-3 extension space of an oriented matroid. The question whether such spaces are spheres or manifolds became the Sturmfels–Ziegler extension space problem, and the low-rank cases are delicate. The notes appear to pose the manifold question directly, in his own language.
missed.quote: Σ=(X,Σ), surface cellulaire des positions relatives X*=Bal(Σ) ... La difficulté conceptuelle ... dans la description de X* au voisinage d'une arête, correspondant à une position sous-stable donnée
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is an unrecorded early, independent approach to extension spaces of pseudo-line arrangements via a sweeping ('balayage') viewpoint. The full dossier might contain an argument for the surface property in rank 3, or a failed one, worth comparing with known results.

missed.claim: He leaves open the rule determining the two endpoint vertices of an edge a_L (the critical positions reached by rotating a sub-stable pseudo-line about its vertex), noting several natural candidate rules, none clearly correct.
missed.quote: L'ennui, c'est qu'il y a plusieurs choix naturels qui viennent à l'esprit, et qu'il n'est pas sûr qu'aucun ...
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is precisely where pseudo-line geometry departs from straight-line geometry. Comparing his candidate rules with combinatorial definitions such as cocircuit signatures or the Goodman–Pollack sweep moves could clarify the issue, but it is likely subsumed by the existing theory.

deep.surprise_reason: The page shows Grothendieck independently constructing what is essentially the extension-space cell complex of a pseudo-line arrangement and pinpointing its delicate local issue. That is a historically interesting parallel to Las Vergnas, Goodman–Pollack and Sturmfels–Ziegler, but nothing here goes beyond known theory, and the key question is left unresolved.
transcription_corrections: 'Bal(Σ)' likely abbreviates 'balayage' (sweep); the reading is plausible but uncertain.
The marginal annotation near 'saisir les deux sommets incidents' is '(?)' over 'deux'; the phrase reads roughly 'saisir les deux (?) sommets incidents à a_L'.

Right column: 'Notons que la donnée d'une orientation superposable de l'arête ... revient à celle d'une orientation de L, celle d'une orientation de a_L à celle d'une orientation superposable au point donnant a ∈ S_L, donc une voie de L en s revient à celle d'une voie de a i.e. d'une des faces incidentes'. 'sous-jacente' in the machine transcription is more likely 'superposable(s)'.

Lower left: 'La difficulté conceptuelle n'est pas dans l'étude locale de X* au voisinage de ρ, en termes de D, ni dans l'étude locale de X* au voisinage d'une face ... mais dans la description de X* au voisinage d'une arête a_L'.
Final words are probably 'qu'il n'est pas sûr qu'aucun d'eux soit le bon' or similar; the machine reading 'droits en mondes' is unreliable.
